opus-5.5.text:
So the headline result, which I think surprised some people, is that GPT-4 is generally more trustworthy than GPT-3.5 on our standard benchmarks. That covers toxicity, stereotype bias, robustness, privacy, machine ethics and fairness. When you just ask it things in the normal way, it does better. That's consistent with what you'd expect from more capable models and more alignment work.

The more interesting finding is what happens under adversarial conditions. When we designed misleading system prompts or jailbreaking-style instructions, GPT-4 was often *more* vulnerable than GPT-3.5. Our interpretation is that this is a side effect of GPT-4 being better at following instructions. It's more faithful to whatever it's told, and that includes instructions that are deliberately trying to get it to produce toxic content, leak private information, or agree with biased statements. So the property that makes it more useful also makes it easier to steer in bad directions.

I think there are a few takeaways. First, trustworthiness isn't a single number. A model can improve on average-case behavior and get worse in the worst case, so you really need to evaluate across many dimensions and threat models. Second, capability and safety don't automatically move together. Sometimes they're in tension, and instruction-following is a really clear example of that. Third, for practitioners, the context you deploy these models in matters a lot. If there's any chance that users or third-party content can inject instructions, the benign-setting numbers can give you false confidence.

More broadly, we see this as an argument for treating evaluation as an ongoing, adversarial process rather than a one-time leaderboard. The models are changing quickly, the ways people try to break them are changing quickly, and we want the evaluations to keep up.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this was the DecodingTrust work, and I think the headline that surprised a lot of people is that it's not a clean story where the newer, bigger model is just better across the board. On most of the perspectives we looked at, toxicity, stereotype bias, adversarial robustness, out-of-distribution robustness, GPT-4 does come out ahead of GPT-3.5 on the standard benchmarks. So in the default setting, it looks more trustworthy, and I think that's real.

But the thing we kept running into is that GPT-4 is also more vulnerable in a specific way. When you give it a system prompt or a user prompt that's adversarially crafted, or even just misleading, GPT-4 follows those instructions more faithfully than GPT-3.5 does. And so it ends up being easier to jailbreak in some of our settings. You can tell it something like, "you're allowed to be toxic now," or you embed a demonstration that nudges it toward leaking information or agreeing with a stereotype, and because it's a better instruction follower, it actually complies more reliably.

So my interpretation is that we're seeing a tradeoff between capability and controllability. The very property that makes GPT-4 more useful, that it understands and follows nuanced instructions, is the same property that an adversary can exploit. Alignment training got it to behave well in the benign case, but that doesn't automatically transfer to the adversarial case, and in some sense the gap between those two got wider.

The other piece I'd emphasize is that these are average-case versus worst-case results. Benchmarks tend to report averages, and averages make GPT-4 look great. Trustworthiness is really about the tail, about what happens when someone is trying to break the system, and there the picture is a lot more mixed. I'd also be careful about over-reading any of this, since these are black-box models, they change over time, and we don't fully know what's in the training data. But I think the broad lesson holds up: you can't infer trustworthiness from capability, you have to measure it directly, and you have to measure it under pressure.

astra-6.text:
The main takeaway is that greater capability doesn’t automatically translate into greater trustworthiness. GPT-4 can improve on GPT-3.5 along some dimensions and still have significant weaknesses along others. So I wouldn’t interpret the comparison as a blanket statement that one model is trustworthy and the other isn’t.

It also matters how you evaluate them. A model might behave well under a straightforward prompt, but that behavior may change when you rephrase the request or actively try to get it to fail. That’s a different question from whether it knows what an appropriate answer looks like.

For me, these evaluations are a way to characterize where we can have confidence and where we need more work. The practical question is: trustworthy for what task, under what conditions, and with what consequences if it gets things wrong?

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main takeaway is that greater capability doesn’t automatically mean greater trustworthiness. You have to ask, trustworthy in what sense, and under what conditions? A model might improve on one dimension and still have weaknesses on another.

And the setup matters. How you prompt the model, what information you give it, and whether someone is actively trying to get it to fail can all affect the outcome. So I wouldn’t interpret a comparison between GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 as a blanket statement that one is trustworthy. It’s evidence about particular behaviors under particular conditions, and we need to be careful about how far we generalize that.
